title: The Towers on the Grass: an Immigrant Engineer, a Governor's Four Years, and Sixty Buildings in the Pampa
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Leonforte, born into the builder's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Spanish and English encyclopedia articles agree on 5 June 1897. Two research passes give slightly different coordinates for the town (37.6389/14.3903 and 37.6497/14.3947); the latter is used here.
stops.campa: On the fifth of June 1897 a son is born in Leonforte, a hill town of the province of Enna, to Salvatore Salamone, architect and builder, and to Antonia D'Anna. He is one of five children in a house where the trade is already part of the furniture: drawing boards, lime, the squaring of walls against a slope. Sicily in these years is emptying westward by the shipload, whole villages drawn off toward the River Plate, and the Salamone family will go with the rest while this child is still small enough to be carried up a gangway.
stops.quote_source: Infobae, coverage of the Rome exhibition of Salamone's work, 21 December 2017
suggested_refs: The parish and civil registers of Leonforte, province of Enna, for June 1897
sources: Infobae, 'Una muestra en Roma homenajea la obra del arquitecto Francisco Salamone, el Gaudí de las pampas', 21 December 2017

stops.name: Puerto de Buenos Aires, the family lands
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the English article gives only 'between 1903 and 1906'; the year shown is the midpoint of that window and appears in no source. Neither ship nor port of embarkation is recorded.
stops.campa: The family lands at the port of Buenos Aires in the first years of the century, among the hundreds of thousands of Italians the Argentine state is counting off the ships and forwarding into the interior. Salvatore goes on building; the boy grows up bilingual in a city raising itself in stone and stucco at a speed no Sicilian town has ever managed. No document reachable now fixes the day, the vessel, or the port they sailed from. The record offers a window of three or four years and nothing tighter than that.
stops.quote: representa también un claro ejemplo de la integración que tuvo la inmigración italiana en la Argentina
stops.quote_source: Tomás Ferrari, Argentine ambassador in Rome, on the 2017 Salamone exhibition, quoted in Infobae, 21 December 2017
suggested_refs: Argentine immigration arrival lists, Puerto de Buenos Aires, 1903-1906

stops.name: Escuela Técnica Otto Krause, the master builder's title
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: attendance is attested (he is listed among the school's distinguished graduates) but no source gives a year. The date shown is a placeholder inside his school years, not a source date.
stops.campa: He is enrolled at the Escuela Técnica Otto Krause on Paseo Colón, the industrial school the republic built so it would not have to import its own technicians, and leaves it with the title of maestro mayor de obras. It is his father's trade in Argentine form: the man licensed to raise the building, not merely to draw it. Salamone keeps the practical half of it all his life and works as contractor as much as designer. For the largest campaign of his career the municipalities will pay him in public works bonds rather than in fees.
suggested_refs: The Otto Krause school register of egresados, Av. Paseo Colón 650, Monserrat

stops.name: La Plata, the contested year at the university
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the stage itself is contested: the Spanish article includes the Universidad Nacional de La Plata, the English article names only Córdoba. Neither gives a year; 1915 is not a source date.
stops.campa: The Spanish account of his schooling sends him next to the National University of La Plata to continue toward the architect's diploma; the English account does not mention La Plata at all and takes him straight to Córdoba. Neither gives a year. What both agree on is the direction of travel: away from the capital, into the provincial universities, toward the double title of architect and civil engineer that will let him sign a structure and also calculate it. The La Plata year, if there was one, has left nothing behind it.
suggested_refs: Student registers of the Universidad Nacional de La Plata, faculty of architecture, 1910s

stops.name: Milan, a medal at the exhibition
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the city; the exhibition is not named and the awarded design is not described.
stops.campa: A design of his is exhibited at Milan and takes a medal. He is a student still, and the award travels back across the Atlantic in the opposite direction to the family: a Sicilian boy's drawing, judged in the north of the country his parents left. Italy in 1919 is full of manifestos and returning soldiers, and its architecture is arguing about speed and concrete. What the design was, and which exhibition hung it, the sources do not say. They say only that there were two medals in one year and that Milan gave one of them.
suggested_refs: Catalogues of the Milan exhibitions of 1919, for the prize lists

stops.name: Barcelona, the second medal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the city; as with Milan, no exhibition is named and no catalogue entry has been located.
stops.campa: The second medal comes from Barcelona in the same year, a city where a cathedral of stone bones has been under construction for thirty-seven years and is nowhere near finished. The medals appear in every account of his life and in no catalogue that can now be checked; neither exhibition is named and neither design is described. Salamone is twenty-two, a student whose drawings take prizes in two European cities within twelve months and whose name means nothing in either of them.
suggested_refs: Prize lists of the Barcelona exhibitions of 1919

stops.name: Córdoba, architect and civil engineer
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, not resolved: the Spanish article gives 1920 as the graduation year, the English article gives 1917. The degrees themselves and the university are attested in both.
stops.campa: He takes his degrees at the National University of Córdoba, architect and civil engineer both, and leaves licensed to design a structure and also to calculate it. Córdoba in these years is the loudest university in the country, a few years past the student reform that turned its governance inside out. The year of the degrees is the first hard contradiction in his record: the Spanish account says 1920, the English says 1917, and nothing reachable adjudicates between them.
suggested_refs: Degree registers of the Universidad Nacional de Córdoba, 1917 and 1920

segments.name: Córdoba, the Practice and the Primary

stops.name: Córdoba province, the first houses
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Spanish article attests private houses and minor works in Córdoba in the early 1920s but gives no year. The date shown is a placeholder within the decade.
stops.campa: Through the twenties he works in the province of Córdoba on private houses and small commissions, the ordinary bread of a young man with two diplomas and no patron. No building from this decade is famous; several are not even dated by the sources that mention them. What he learns here is a method rather than a style: how to price a job, and how to move material to a town without a railhead before the money changes character. He is in his twenties, and nothing he puts up in these years is photographed.
suggested_refs: Municipal building permits of Córdoba province, 1920s, for works signed Salamone

stops.name: Córdoba, the primary he loses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the contest; the pin is the city of Córdoba, since the seat sought was that of the Punilla department in the same province and no single site is recorded.
stops.campa: He stands in an internal contest of the Unión Cívica Radical for a provincial senate seat, the department of Punilla in the Córdoba sierras, and loses it. The episode is one line in his biography: no source gives the vote, the rival, or the platform. Everything he builds afterward is built for other men's offices and on other men's mandates, and the party he ran under holds nothing in Buenos Aires province when his real work begins there. It is the only time in his life that he seeks office himself.
suggested_refs: Unión Cívica Radical internal election records, Córdoba province, 1923

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Adolfina Croft
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the marriage; the place is given by no source. The English article says only that Adolfina Croft was the daughter of the Austro-Hungarian vice-consul stationed at Bahía Blanca, so siting the wedding there would be inference; the canonical Buenos Aires pin (inherited from victoria_ocampo.journey.json) is used instead.
stops.campa: He marries Adolfina Croft, of Austrian descent, daughter of the Austro-Hungarian vice-consul posted at Bahía Blanca, in a country then full of consular families with no state left to report to. Four children follow: Ricardo, Roberto, Ana María, Stella Maris. Of the household almost nothing is recorded. The same sources that catalogue sixty public buildings down to the month give the marriage a year and no city, and give the wife her father's title and not one word of her own.
suggested_refs: Argentine civil marriage registers for 1928 under the names Salamone and Croft

stops.name: Las Varillas, the first municipal palace
stops.date_confidence: attested: the works annex dates the Las Varillas municipal building from May 1935 to 22 March 1936. An earlier research pass gave the range as 1934-1936, which belongs to the Villa María works instead.
stops.campa: In Las Varillas, a wheat town in eastern Córdoba, he raises a municipal building from May 1935 and finishes it on the twenty-second of March 1936. The town has a few thousand inhabitants and now has a skyline. It is the first work at the scale he will be known for, and everything he builds in Buenos Aires province across the next four years is already in it: a civic front too large for its plaza, vertical masses stepping up into a tower, ornament cut into the concrete rather than applied over it.
suggested_refs: The Municipalidad of Las Varillas, Córdoba, completed 22 March 1936

stops.name: Villa María, the slaughterhouse in Córdoba
stops.date_confidence: attested within a range: the works annex brackets the Villa María works between 1934 and 1936 and does not narrow them further.
stops.campa: At Villa María on the Tercero river he builds the municipal slaughterhouse, the second of the Córdoba public works and the first matadero in a career that will produce a dozen. The building type is the least ceremonial in a town's inventory, a shed where animals are killed under municipal inspection. Salamone gives it a facade. By the time he leaves Córdoba he has proved to two intendentes that a small budget can buy a monument. The province he goes to next is five hundred kilometres east.
suggested_refs: The Matadero Municipal of Villa María, Córdoba

stops.name: La Plata, Fresco takes the province
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date of Fresco's assumption of office; the commissioning relationship with Salamone is documented, the personal friendship is not.
stops.campa: Manuel Fresco takes the governorship of Buenos Aires province on the eighteenth of February 1936, under a motto of three words and a public works law that lets the province borrow against bonds to build in its towns. The declared aim is to dignify the official and scenic profile of the region. Within months the commission is Salamone's. Whether the two men were friends is repeated everywhere and verified nowhere: the encyclopedia that carries the claim states plainly that it has not been possible to prove, and no letter between them has surfaced.
stops.quote_source: The motto of Governor Manuel Fresco's 1936 public works plan, quoted in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The Buenos Aires provincial public works bond law of 1936, under which the campaign was financed
sources: Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002

stops.name: Balcarce, the portal of the cemetery
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (works annex, Balcarce cementerio 1936); no month recorded.
stops.campa: At Balcarce, inland from Mar del Plata under the last hills of the Tandilia, he builds the portal of the town cemetery, among the earliest works of the provincial campaign. The gate is the whole architecture: a screen of concrete thrown across the entrance, taller than anything behind it, so that the dead are approached through a facade with nothing but graves on its far side. Over the next four years he will build the same argument in half a dozen towns, each time with a different figure standing on top of it.
suggested_refs: The cemetery portal of Balcarce, Buenos Aires province, 1936

stops.name: Balcarce, the wedding cake in the plaza
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fountain and the nickname (Forn, 2002) and for Plaza Libertad at Balcarce in 1936 (works annex). Contradiction flagged: the municipal palace the fountain is said to face appears only in the English article's undifferentiated list and not in the detailed Spanish annex, which lists seven other Balcarce works.
stops.campa: Facing the municipal building at Balcarce he sets a fountain, tiered and white, stepping upward in rings. The town looks at it and names it: la torta de bodas, the wedding cake. His provincial work collects nicknames like this wherever it lands, half admiration and half the countryside's refusal to be impressed by a thing it did not ask for. The plaza around it, Plaza Libertad, is dated 1936 in the annex, together with a rural normal school and delegation buildings at Los Pinos and San Agustín.
stops.quote_source: What the townspeople of Balcarce called the fountain Salamone built facing the municipal palace, in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The fountain on Plaza Libertad, Balcarce
sources: Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002

stops.name: Guaminí, the palace beside the lagoon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; no month recorded. The saying quoted is dated only to the building years, roughly 1936-1940.
stops.campa: The municipal palace of Guaminí goes up beside another lagoon in the same southwest, another town of a few thousand souls given a vertical civic front that is visible from the road before the town itself is. Across the province a saying starts up in these years, repeated in the towns and then in the press: what Fresco orders, Salamone builds. It is not quite true, and the province produces its own correction to it soon enough, but it describes what the roads look like between 1936 and 1940.
stops.quote: Lo que Fresco dispone lo construye Salamone
stops.quote_source: Popular saying in Buenos Aires province during the building years, quoted in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal and Matadero of Guaminí

stops.name: Rauch, the palace and the unstable count
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year. Numeric contradiction flagged: the English article's works section says more than sixty buildings across twenty-five rural districts, while the figure seventy appears elsewhere inside the same article; the Spanish article says more than sixty.
stops.campa: At Rauch he builds the municipal palace, one of more than sixty buildings the campaign puts into some twenty-five districts of the province in four years. The count is itself unstable: the same English article that says more than sixty in one section says more than seventy in another, and no independent inventory reconciles the two. What is not in dispute is the pace. Salamone is running a construction company and a design office at once, moving crews across four hundred kilometres of pampa, finishing buildings in months.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Rauch, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Coronel Pringles, the palace and the slaughterhouse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year in both editions of his catalogue; no month given for either building.
stops.campa: Coronel Pringles receives both halves of the program in 1937: the municipal palace on the plaza and the slaughterhouse out on the edge of town. They are the same architecture. The building where the town's business is transacted and the building where its meat is inspected get the same concrete verticals and the same stepped mass, and a citizen who has seen one of them has already been told what to expect of the other. Both are listed in both editions of his catalogue, in each case without a month.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal and Matadero of Coronel Pringles

stops.name: Alberti, the tower sized against the horizon
stops.date_confidence: attested within a range: the works annex dates the Alberti municipal building 1937-1938. Coordinates corrected: an earlier pass placed the town twenty kilometres west of where it stands.
stops.campa: At Alberti, on the western road out of Buenos Aires, the municipal palace is built across 1937 and 1938. There is no plaza in the province large enough for what Salamone puts on it, and he does not adjust: the tower is sized against the horizon rather than against the block. He leaves no theory of his own and never publishes a line explaining what he is doing, so a professor of architecture will later have to coin a name for the whole manner. The annex records nothing else about the building.
stops.quote_source: Prof. Mario Sabugo's coinage for Salamone's style, quoted in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Alberti, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Pellegrini, the palace and the misnamed town
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (works annex: Pellegrini, municipalidad and matadero, 1937). Source error flagged: the English article calls the town Carlos Pellegrini, which is a different place in Santa Fe, and the mistake has propagated into coordinates roughly 185 kilometres off.
stops.campa: At Pellegrini, on the national road five hundred kilometres from the capital, he builds the municipal palace and the slaughterhouse in the same year. The town's name causes a durable confusion in his catalogue: one English account calls it Carlos Pellegrini, which is a different town in a different province, and the error has been copied onto maps that place these buildings nearly two hundred kilometres away in open country. The buildings are in Pellegrini, seat of the Pellegrini district, where they have stood since 1937.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal and Matadero of Pellegrini, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Puan, the charge over the southwest
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a Puan municipal palace is listed in the biographical articles but not in the detailed works annex, and no year is given anywhere. The date shown falls inside the campaign, not on a source.
stops.campa: Puan is listed among his municipal palaces in both editions of his biography and in neither of the detailed annexes, which is how a good deal of his catalogue stands. The charge he is given over this corner of the province is to consolidate it in urban terms, a phrase quoted without a decree behind it. In practice it means arriving in a town on a lagoon in the dry southwest, choosing the most visible ground, and leaving a mass of concrete on it. Whether anyone in Puan was asked first is not recorded.
stops.quote_source: Phrase describing the charge Fresco gave Salamone over the province's southwest, quoted in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Puan, Buenos Aires province, attribution unverified in the works annex

stops.name: Laprida, the town given three buildings
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the works annex assigns the Laprida municipal palace, slaughterhouse and cemetery portal all to 1937, without months.
stops.campa: The municipal palace of Laprida rises in 1937 in a district of sheep and wheat with fewer than ten thousand inhabitants. Salamone builds it, its slaughterhouse and its cemetery portal in the same campaign, so that the three points at which the town meets its own government are all in one hand and in one idiom. The annex assigns all three to 1937 and gives no month for any of them. He is thirty-nine or forty, depending on which graduation year is believed.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Laprida, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Carhué, the palace inaugurated
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the inauguration (3 December 1938); the works annex dates construction 1937-1938. The 2014 national monument declaration is attested in the article on Carhué.
stops.campa: The Palacio Municipal of Carhué opens on the third of December 1938 on the edge of a salt lake in the province's southwest, its tower standing over a town of a few thousand where fifty years earlier there was a fort on a ditch dug across the plain to stop cattle raids. The writers who catalogue the building name three idioms in its mass: Art Deco, the Italian Futurism of Marinetti's manifestos, and a functionalism out of the Bauhaus. Argentina declares it a national historic monument in 2014.
stops.quote: apenas 50 años antes, el pueblo aún no era sino un caserío en torno a un fuerte militar, sobre la Zanja de Alsina. Con la llegada de los colonos europeos y del ferrocarril se produjo un progreso enorme en muy poco tiempo, simbolizado de algún modo en el osado Palacio Municipal
stops.quote_source: Gastón Partarrieu, director of the local museum at Carhué, quoted in Graciela Cutuli, 'La ruta de Salamone', Página/12, Turismo, 3 May 2015
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Carhué, national historic monument since 2014
sources: Graciela Cutuli, 'La ruta de Salamone', Página/12, Turismo, 3 May 2015

stops.name: Laprida, the cross taken off the train
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the portal. The interception scene comes from Forn's 2002 article and is not corroborated elsewhere. Superlative flagged: the biographical article calls the cross the second highest religious work in South America after the Cristo Redentor, while the article on Laprida claims only the second highest cross, thirty metres. No measurement source settles either version.
stops.campa: The frontispiece of the Laprida cemetery is fabricated in pieces and loaded onto a train. The town's intendente, a caudillo named Martínez, meets the wagons and stops them: the cemetery stays here. The pieces come off at gunpoint, by the account that survives, and the portal is raised at Laprida with its monumental cross and its full-length crucified Christ. Circulating writeups call it the second highest religious work in South America after the Cristo Redentor; the town's own entry claims only the second highest cross, thirty metres.
stops.quote_source: The intendente of Laprida, a man named Martínez, intercepting the train carrying the cemetery frontispiece, in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The cemetery portal and cross of Laprida, Buenos Aires province
sources: Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002

stops.name: Saldungaray, the Christ inside the circle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (works annex: Saldungaray cementerio 1937, matadero 1937). Coordinates corrected: two earlier passes placed the village ten and seventeen kilometres from where it stands.
stops.campa: Saldungaray is not a municipality; it is a village in the district of Tornquist under the sierra, and it holds one of the most photographed things Salamone ever built. The portal of its cemetery is a great ring set upright on the ground with a crucified Christ inside it, the circle opened at the base for the road to pass through. He builds the village slaughterhouse in the same year. More than one account of his work prints the village in the wrong place, ten and seventeen kilometres off its real position.
suggested_refs: The circular cemetery portal of Saldungaray, partido de Tornquist

stops.name: Salliqueló, the gate and the shed
stops.date_confidence: attested within a range: the works annex dates the Salliqueló cemetery portal and slaughterhouse 1937-1938. Coordinates corrected: an earlier pass placed the town about sixty-five kilometres south of its real position.
stops.campa: At Salliqueló, in the province's northwest corner near the La Pampa line, he builds the cemetery portal and the slaughterhouse across 1937 and 1938. The pair is the standard delivery of the campaign to a small town: the gate the dead go through and the shed the cattle go through, both signed, both in concrete, both taller than the grain silos. Neither is on the plaza. Both stand at the edge of town, where the roads out begin, and the annex dates them together without giving a month for either.
suggested_refs: The cemetery portal and slaughterhouse of Salliqueló

stops.name: Carhué, the Cristo del Lago
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, not resolved: the works annex enters the Carhué cross under 1938, while the article on Carhué says it was emplaced in 1937, made with the sculptor Santiago Chierico. There is no Salamone cemetery portal at Carhué; earlier passes that reported one were in error.
stops.campa: Above the shore of Lake Epecuén he raises a monumental cross with the sculptor Santiago Chierico, the figure the town calls the Cristo del Lago. The lake below it is salt, and it is rising: within fifty years that water will drown the resort seven kilometres away and leave this cross among the few things in the district still standing clear above it. The sources disagree about the year by one. The works annex enters the cross under 1938; Carhué's own account says it was set in place in 1937.
suggested_refs: The Cristo del Lago at Carhué, made with the sculptor Santiago Chierico

stops.name: Azul, the archangel over the gate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the works annex year; the figure over the gate is described in the Spanish article as the archangel Gabriel, elsewhere as an angel of death. Coordinates for the Azul cemetery differ between research passes by about three kilometres.
stops.campa: Over the gate of the Azul cemetery he sets the archangel, wings flattened into the concrete, and beneath it the letters RIP cast at the scale of a building rather than a headstone. A specialist calls the complex an obra total, the one phrase the record offers for what Salamone does when a town hands him a whole site instead of a facade. The angel faces the road in. Whoever comes to bury someone at Azul walks toward it for several hundred metres before reaching the gate.
stops.quote_source: Alejandro Novacovsky on the Azul cemetery complex, quoted in Graciela Cutuli, 'La ruta de Salamone', Página/12, Turismo, 3 May 2015
suggested_refs: The cemetery portal of Azul with its archangel figure
sources: Graciela Cutuli, 'La ruta de Salamone', Página/12, Turismo, 3 May 2015

stops.name: Pilar, the portal near the capital
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (works annex: Pilar cementerio 1938, Plaza San Martín 1938). Correction noted: Pilar is a district of Greater Buenos Aires about fifty kilometres from the capital, not of the provincial interior.
stops.campa: At Pilar, fifty kilometres from the capital, he builds the portal of the cemetery and works on the Plaza San Martín, both dated 1938. It is the least remote place in his provincial catalogue, a district of the Buenos Aires periphery rather than of the deep pampa, close enough that a man could come out from the city in a morning to see it. He will be buried in this same district twenty-one years later, and nothing in the record says he chose it. He is forty-one.
suggested_refs: The cemetery portal of Pilar and the Plaza San Martín, both 1938

stops.name: Villa Epecuén, the slaughterhouse by the salt lake
stops.date_confidence: attested: the works annex dates the Villa Epecuén slaughterhouse from 1937 to 3 December 1938. Coordinates corrected: earlier passes placed the resort sixteen to eighteen kilometres from its real position, and one pass duplicated this building as a separate matadero at Carhué town.
stops.campa: Seven kilometres from Carhué, at the lakeside resort of Villa Epecuén, he builds the slaughterhouse between 1937 and its completion on the third of December 1938. The resort has thermal salt water, hotels and trains from the capital. On the tenth of November 1985 the lake breaks its embankment and takes the town; the water stands over it for a quarter of a century before it withdraws. What comes back out of the salt is a grid of bleached ruins with Salamone's building at the entrance to it.
suggested_refs: The Matadero of Villa Epecuén, standing at the entrance to the flooded town

stops.name: Tornquist, the pair under the sierra
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of the slaughterhouse in the works annex; the municipal palace is attested in both biographical articles without a month.
stops.campa: Tornquist sits at the foot of the Sierra de la Ventana, and Salamone builds it a municipal palace and a slaughterhouse. The town was founded by a banker and laid out around a plaza with some ambition in it, one of the few places in the campaign where the new civic architecture has something to answer to. He answers it in concrete regardless. From the road the tower reads against the sierra; the slaughterhouse stands lower and further out, past the last street of the town.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal and Matadero of Tornquist, under the Sierra de la Ventana

stops.name: Chillar, the delegation building
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year (works annex: Delegación de Chillar, 1937, listed under Azul). Source error flagged: the English article lists Chillar as having a municipal palace, which is impossible, since Chillar is a locality of the Azul district and has no municipality of its own.
stops.campa: Chillar has no municipality of its own; it is a locality of the Azul district, and what Salamone builds there in 1937 is a delegation, the branch office through which a district government reaches a town that is not its seat. English accounts of his work list it flatly as a municipal palace, which it cannot have been. He builds the slaughterhouse as well. The delegation is the smallest ceremonial commission in the campaign and it gets the same treatment as the largest. The annex files both works under Azul.
suggested_refs: The municipal delegation building of Chillar, partido de Azul, 1937

stops.name: Vedia, the meat first and the government after
stops.date_confidence: attested: the works annex dates the Vedia slaughterhouse to 1937 and the municipal building to 1938. Coordinates corrected: earlier passes placed the town about thirty-eight kilometres west of its real position.
stops.campa: Vedia, in the district of Leandro N. Alem in the north of the province, receives the slaughterhouse in 1937 and the municipal palace the year after. The order of delivery is worth recording: the meat first, the government second. Coordinates for the town have been published nearly forty kilometres west of where it actually stands, which is another way of saying that for a long time nobody drove out to check. Both buildings are on the Vedia grid, at the edge of the wheat country.
suggested_refs: The Matadero (1937) and Palacio Municipal (1938) of Vedia, partido de Leandro N. Alem

stops.name: Azul, the matadero that outlives its trade
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of construction. The conversion into the Centro Cultural Salamone is reported in the biographical articles but no reachable source dates it; the building's own encyclopedia page returned an error when fetched.
stops.campa: The municipal slaughterhouse of Azul is the most photographed industrial building of the campaign: a long horizontal block with a tower, arcades, and lettering cut into the concrete, standing at the edge of a town of some thirty thousand. Food sanitation is a live political question in these years, and the museum director at Carhué sets out the logic of the whole program in one sentence. Decommissioned, the building survives, restored and reopened as the Centro Cultural Salamone; no reachable source gives the date of the conversion.
stops.quote: plan de construcción de edificios que representaba las funciones de los gobiernos locales: los palacios municipales, los cementerios y los mataderos, porque hay que recordar que la sanidad alimentaria era una preocupación que se hizo prioritaria en aquellos tiempos
stops.quote_source: Gastón Partarrieu, quoted in Graciela Cutuli, 'La ruta de Salamone', Página/12, Turismo, 3 May 2015
suggested_refs: The former Matadero Municipal of Azul, now the Centro Cultural Salamone
sources: Graciela Cutuli, 'La ruta de Salamone', Página/12, Turismo, 3 May 2015

segments.name: The Last Works of the Program

stops.name: Adolfo Gonzales Chaves, a late palace
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year in the works annex; no month recorded.
stops.campa: By 1939 the campaign is running out of years. At Adolfo Gonzales Chaves, in the south of the province, he builds the municipal palace, among the last of the palaces. The bond machinery that funded the program is under strain and the governor's term has a fixed end on it, while Salamone is still delivering buildings at a rate his contemporaries in the capital find difficult to credit. He is forty-two. The palace goes up on the plaza of a district of some eleven thousand people spread across six thousand square kilometres of grass.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Adolfo Gonzales Chaves

stops.name: Chascomús, the last palace
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year in the works annex; the counter-saying quoted is dated only to the building years.
stops.campa: Chascomús, on its lagoon a hundred kilometres from the capital, takes delivery of its municipal palace in 1940, among the last works of the program. The province has meanwhile produced a correction to its own saying, crediting the ubiquitous Alejandro Bustillo instead, whose hotels and casinos are going up in the same years across the same country. Two men are being credited with building Argentina in this decade, and everybody in the towns can name them both. Neither saying can be dated beyond the building years, and neither has an author.
stops.quote: No se mueve un ladrillo sin que lo diga Bustillo
stops.quote_source: The corrective counter-saying to the Fresco and Salamone one, quoted in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The Palacio Municipal of Chascomús, 1940

stops.name: La Plata, the governorship ends
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the end of Fresco's term; the building totals carry the 60 versus 70 discrepancy noted at Rauch.
stops.campa: Fresco's term ends on the seventh of March 1940 and the commission ends with it. In four years the province has taken delivery of more than sixty buildings across some twenty-five districts, put up, in the summarizing account, with a quality unique for the time in which it was done. No successor continues the program. Salamone is forty-two and at the top of a practice with no client left in it. The totals themselves do not agree: sixty in one section of the English account, seventy in another.
stops.quote: dignificar el perfil oficial y paisajista de la región
stops.quote_source: Stated goal of Fresco's provincial building plan, quoted in Juan Forn, 'El misterio de la piedra líquida', Página/12, Radar, 2 June 2002
suggested_refs: The provincial public works accounts of the Fresco administration, 1936-1940

segments.name: Tucumán, Montevideo, and the Grave at Pilar

stops.name: San Miguel de Tucumán, the paving contract
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year and the nature of the dispute; the charges, the court and the parties are not described in any reachable source.
stops.campa: A paving contract in the city of San Miguel de Tucumán turns into a case against him in 1943. The record of the dispute is thin to the point of transparency: a paving job, a legal action, a lawyer's advice to leave the country while it is pending. Salamone leaves. He is forty-six, the most prolific public architect the province of Buenos Aires has ever employed, and he crosses out of Argentina over a street contract in the north. What the state alleged, and what he answered, is in no account reachable now.
suggested_refs: Court records of the Tucumán paving case, 1943

stops.name: Montevideo, the years outside the country
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to the city: the Spanish article says only that he lived in Uruguay for the duration of the case. Montevideo is the researcher's assumption and is asserted as attested in one earlier pass, which is not supportable.
stops.campa: He passes the years of the case outside Argentina, in Uruguay. Where in Uruguay is stated by no source; Montevideo is an assumption, made because it is the country's one large city and the natural refuge for a Buenos Aires professional across the river. He is not building. The buildings he did build are already going out of fashion in the capital's schools, which by the middle forties are arguing about a rationalism with no ornament in it at all.
suggested_refs: Uruguayan residence records for Salamone, 1943-1945, not located

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the case won
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of return and the outcome of the claim; the canonical Buenos Aires pin is inherited unchanged.
stops.campa: He wins his claim against the state over unpaid professional fees and returns to Buenos Aires in 1945; the charges against him are afterward dismissed. He is forty-eight. The practice he resumes is a city practice, paving contracts and private clients, and it bears no resemblance to what he did between 1936 and 1940. Nothing in the record says what the two years abroad cost him, or whether anyone in the fifty towns he built in wrote to him while he was gone. The judgment itself is reproduced nowhere reachable.
suggested_refs: The judgment in Salamone's claim against the Argentine state, 1945

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Rationalist decade
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the post-war Rationalist work is attested but undated; the English article spreads it across the 1950s. The year shown is a placeholder inside that decade.
stops.campa: In the years after his return he directs urban paving works and designs in the Rationalist manner: two buildings and a private house, and by some accounts a further run of residential condominiums through the fifties. None of it is precisely dated in the sources and none of it is photographed the way the province's slaughterhouses are. The ornament is gone. The man who cut angels and crosses into concrete for a governor spends his last working decade on flat facades. No address has been identified for any of these buildings.
suggested_refs: The post-1945 Rationalist buildings attributed to Salamone in Buenos Aires, unidentified by address

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death at sixty-two
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in both editions; the age of sixty-two follows from the 1897 birth.
stops.campa: Francisco Salamone dies in Buenos Aires on the eighth of August 1959, aged sixty-two. He has published nothing explaining his work and given no interview that survives in the reachable record. No manifesto has ever turned up, and no theoretical writing of any kind in his own hand. The obituary attention is slight. Nineteen years after the last palace his buildings stand in fifty towns, towers up, whitewashed in some places and roofless in others. The first scholarly article on them is thirty-three years away.
suggested_refs: Buenos Aires civil death register, 8 August 1959

stops.name: Pilar, the grave and the contradiction
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, not resolved: the Spanish article buries him directly at the Cementerio Jardín de Paz in Pilar, the English article buries him first at Recoleta and has him transferred to Jardín de Paz later, with no date for the move. The day shown is the day after death, not a source date, and the pin is the Pilar town point rather than the cemetery, whose exact site could not be verified.
stops.campa: He is buried in the Cementerio Jardín de Paz at Pilar, in the district where he built a cemetery portal twenty-one years earlier. The two accounts of the burial do not agree: one puts him at Jardín de Paz from the start, the other has him first at Recoleta in the capital and transferred out here later, and gives no date for the move. The exact site of the grave could not be verified. In 2001 the province declares his works its cultural patrimony; by 2014 several of them are national historic monuments.
suggested_refs: Alberto Bellucci, 'Monumental Art Deco in the Pampas: The Urban Art of Francisco Salamone', The Journal of Decorative and Propaganda Arts (1992)
Tom Shaw and Edward Shaw, Salamone, La Consagración (2007)
